source.title: Ridge interpolators in correlated factor regression models - exact risk analysis

record.tranche_reason: The paper derives and simulates interpolation and risk behavior in correlated factor regression models. It discusses neural-network generalization as motivation, but does not test any listed version on the specified networks or settings.
record.gate_note: The paper's own FRM results concern excess prediction risk and interpolation. They do not test the network behaviors named in V1–V8; cited neural-network findings are not this paper's results.
record.test_reason: The study derives and simulates prediction risk for linear factor regression estimators. It discusses neural-network interpolation as motivation, but its own results do not test any behavior named in V1–V8. Increasing a feature-to-sample ratio in factor regression does not test widening trained ReLU networks in V2.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors derive precise risk characterizations for GLS, LS, and ridge in correlated factor regression, report close agreement with simulations, and conclude that optimally tuned ridge smooths double descent but offers limited improvement above ratios around 5 and virtually none above 10 in their examples. They interpret this as extending interpolation's predictive usefulness beyond neural networks.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes classical linear factor regression estimators using Random Duality Theory and numerical simulations, rather than training neural networks or fitting random labels.
record.method_sensitivity: The risk depends on over-parametrization ratio and model parameters, including covariance matrices, loadings, and dimensions; the paper also reports different behavior under uncorrelated and correlated setups.

fits_no_version.finding: Factor regression exhibits double descent across LS and minimum-norm interpolation regimes. At feature-to-sample ratio 3, GLS has zero training residual and excess risk 0.3205, below the null baseline of 1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Minimum-norm interpolation can predict better than the null predictor in factor regression, with risk depending on dimensional ratios, covariance structure, and loading scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimally tuned ridge smooths factor-regression double descent; its advantage becomes small at high over-parameterization in the reported examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ridge regularization can improve factor-regression prediction risk near interpolation while providing little advantage at sufficiently high over-parameterization.

record.problems: The paper's numerical results use finite simulated dimensions; its network-related statements are contextual rather than direct network experiments. No uncertainty intervals are reported for the simulation table values.
record.rows_left_out: No rows from the paper's broader estimator-quantity analyses were included because they do not measure the neural-network behaviors in V1–V8.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-versus-random-label held-out accuracy in neural networks.
Test error as trained ReLU networks widen beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout effects on classifier test error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of neural-network generalization gaps.
Test accuracy after removing memorized versus randomly selected training examples.

record.verdict_notes: States are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because all rows concern a different system. This does not dispute the reported factor-regression findings. No additional results testing a listed version appear in the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: The specified neural networks, random-label fitting, and natural-label test accuracy.
Width sweeps of the specified ReLU networks.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Dropout interventions in the specified classifiers.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to gaps across the specified networks.
Removing memorized examples and measuring test accuracy.

rows.subject: GLS interpolator
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed excess prediction risk as a function of the over-parametrization ratio in a correlated factor regression model.
rows.value: The GLS excess prediction risk exhibits double-descent behavior.
rows.note: This is an FRM result, not a neural-network test.
rows.check: The result concerns factor regression, so it cannot establish a listed version's effect. The full double-descent curve combines LS below interpolation with GLS above it; GLS alone is defined only in the over-parameterized regime. Section 5.1 also shows that GLS risk can eventually rise within that regime.

source_check.locator_found: Abstract; Section 2.3, p. 9; Section 2.2.3; Section 6, p. 38.

rows.subject: Optimally tuned ridge estimator
rows.operation_detail: Compared excess prediction risk across over-parametrization ratios with the GLS interpolator.
rows.value: Ridge regularization can smooth the double-descent behavior; the smoothing effect is described as limited above over-parametrization ratios of 5 and virtually nonexistent above 10.
rows.note: The stated thresholds are over-parametrization ratios.
rows.check: The ridge-versus-GLS risk comparison is a factor regression result, outside V1–V8. The thresholds of 5 and 10 describe the reported examples and should not be presented as universal guarantees.

rows.subject: GLS interpolator

conditions.value: uncorrelated factors and noise; scaled unitary loadings

rows.baseline: Null-risk shown in Figure 2; exact value not stated
rows.note: Table reports theoretical/simulated values; the GLS has zero in-sample risk at this setting.
rows.check: The theoretical/simulated excess risks of 0.3205/0.3205 and zero training residual are correctly recorded, but do not measure a listed version. The null excess-risk baseline is 1 under this setup's identity factor covariance and unit-norm coefficient vector.
